children: Boeing stock fell more than 2% Thursday morning, as investors fretted over reports that the summit between President Trump and Chinese President Xi was unlikely to yield a new order for the commercial jet maker.
Boeing didn't immediately comment on the reports. It likely won't have much to add about order speculation.
Shares were down 2.3% at $195.07, while S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were off 0.5% and 0.3%, respectively.

China comes up from time to time for Boeing, for good reason. Still, it seems to loom unnecessarily large in investors' minds. There are other things to worry about, including production rates, new plane certification, and fuel prices.

The country, of course, matters. China has a large and growing market for air travel, making it a key source of demand for both Boeing and Airbus. China will need an estimated 9,000 new planes over the coming 20 years.

That demand, however, isn't reflected in Boeing's current order book. China accounts for about 2% of the backlog of undelivered aircraft. (Boeing has "undefined" customers in its backlog, too. Some of those aircraft are likely for China.) That's low. China accounted for roughly 20% of Boeing deliveries from 2010 to 2019.

China hasn't ordered many planes lately in the aftermath of Covid-19. Order rates have picked up, but they favor Airbus, with Boeing impacted by trade tensions and its 737 MAX problems. Between 2010 and 2019, Boeing could expect more than 100 firm orders from Chinese airlines each year-similar to Airbus. That's dropped to almost nothing, until a framework agreement with China (which isn't a firm order) for 200 jets in May.

Boeing getting frozen out of the Chinese market certainly sounds ominous. But it should eventually win its fair share of the business, if for no other reason than Airbus and China's own plane maker COMAC may not be able to supply all the demand.

China is a niggling issue, but it should resolve as Boeing continues its turnaround under CEO Kelly Ortberg. Key to the turnaround is boosting plane production. Boeing shipped more than 800 jets in 2018, the year before the second fatal 737 MAX crash. It hasn't come close to that number since. Wall Street expects 800-plus deliveries in 2028, which should translate into roughly $10 billion in free cash flow.

Production is the single biggest issue facing Boeing and Boeing stock. Shares dipped recently after Ortberg said the ramp-up in 737 MAX production was going slowly at a conference in September. BofA analyst Ron Epstein called the stock dip an "overreaction to predictable headwinds," adding, "production challenges should be expected. It's Boeing, they make airplanes, and the turnaround will take time."

Oil prices are another concern. Higher oil prices lead to higher jet fuel prices, which can raise ticket prices and reduce demand for air travel. Boeing stock was above $230 shortly before the Iran war began. It traded below $190 in late March as oil prices soared.

China probably ranks a distant third, or fourth, on the list of current issues. Boeing also needs to certify its 777X and 737 MAX-10 jets for commercial service. Chinese demand is also softened by Boeing's current backlog of unfilled orders, which sits at almost 6,800 planes.
